then Louise capitulated, made up her mind, broke open the rubber ring, opening a notebook at ran¬ dom, examining without surprise (for she knew this, too, before even opening it: that she would find here neither journal nor memoirs nor yellowed letters nor anything of the kind: that is, anything that might betray some quality of impropriety—and not even impropriety: of absurdity, of nonsense, for these were the sorts of ideas (keeping a journal, writing the story of her own life) which could not even have occurred to the woman who had written here) the pages uniformly divided into three columns, the two on the right headed by the inevitable and sempiternal captions: Credits, Debits, that on the left, wider, reserved for descriptions, the ink faded, yellowed at the same time as the paper, letters and figures written by a firm hand in that schoolgirl handwriting, with the thick and thin strokes imperturbably formed, unyielding, as though depersonal¬ ized, stamped too with that inflexible modesty which re¬ fused all commentary, having no other concern and no other justification than to be readable (as doubtless the first quality of good manners, elementary self-respect and respect for others, is expressed by the concern to be clean and decently dressed at all times, and this not to bear witness, to testify before some imaginary tribunal or some imaginary posterity, but simply because the corollary of 101 decent clothes, of cleanliness, was that these things (debits, credits, trips, illnesses, hay sales or deaths) were, for the sake of order, written down, in their time and in their place, and nothing more—, reading then at random: JANUARY 1 Cash on hand. 700 4 Our two salaries. 1445 6 Pierre sick, Eugenie sends 800 Fr. for his trip to Bordeaux. 800 7 The bank has remitted all the 6% bonds I had sent in last June. 102 12 An umbrella. 32 14 Sold 3 bushels of nuts @ 1550 a bushel . 4650 17 Man for shovelling snow. 20 23 Received from M. Debourg, wood- seller, 90 Fr. for indemnity (Bru de Corne field) . 90 25 Eugenie home with 560 Fr. ... 560 the trivial events (and not even events: facts, incidents— and not even incidents: the everyday, the commonplace -—and not even trivial: minuscule, insignificant) rising again to the surface of time, of the past, like pilings stuck here and there in the gray immensity that had no begin¬ ning or end, their insignificance, their very tininess, out of all proportion with the frame in which they were set, according them a kind of unexpected grandeur, a majesty, the inflexible, impersonal regular handwriting enumer- 102 ating, recapitulating, adding not debits or credits that could be assessed in terms of cash and decimals but, so to speak, the immemorial and invariable entities: for food, for clothing, for heat, and the snow suddenly one winter morning, and the immemorial clatter or shovels on the sidewalks, and the immemorial accounts of fences collapsing, boundary-posts knocked over, the immemorial constraints: hunger, sickness, clothing, everything, page after page, year after year, Louise turning through thick¬ nesses of time, reading again: Guillaumot has cut down the cherry trees, which yielded cords of wood. He asks 9 Fr. 6/2 @ cord, which makes 58 Fr. 50 for the whole 1/2 job. He has asked me to give him 18 Fr. 50 and since he is renting the orchard at 140 Fr. he will owe 100 Fr. for this year. 18,50 and again: Yesterday Pierre, Sabine, and the children left; expenditure during this month for feeding six people. 1.365 all on the same level—wood yields, vacations, departures, grocers' bills or doctors' fees—; not tragedy, screams, the accidental, the spectacular, but what constitutes, so to speak, the very warp of existence, as if (just as in those letters soldiers write or receive in which are found, despite the grammar school education, neither punctuation nor capitals) some secret knowledge, that rigorous experience 103 which needs neither books nor eloquence, had led the hand through all these pages, had taught it not to make distinctions between the fact—the obligation—of decor¬ ating graves, of wearing a dress, or of dying, writing: SEPTEMBER 18 Purchase and transportation of 6 items of canned goods. 31.50 24 Eugenie (underlined twice, the second time in red pencil) 25 Newspaper subscription. 48 and on the next page: OCTOBER 16 Rental of the Ferriere field. 40 20 Eugenie died (written in pencil) 25 Funeral announcements. 70 Hearse. 100 Two carriages @ 25 Fr. 50 Coffin. 100 29 Bill from Godin (gutter and chimney weathercock) . 50 370 40 and later, when Louise remembered that period—the ten days that passed this way in the tepid agony of the dying summer—it appeared to her not like a specific slice of time, measurable and limited, but as a vague, criss-crossed interval, composed of a succession, an alternation of ups 104 and downs, of darks and lights: the closed room, the blind¬ ing light outside, the fierce and exuberant September vegetation, the darkness, the mummified face, the glory, the peace of the waning days-—seeing herself, able to see the bright dress running across the screen of her mem¬ ory, the luminous spot, followed by the projector's beam, rushing down the green slope or perhaps not running: walking slowly, in any case until after the chestnut trees with their already yellowing leaves, ringed, attacked by a rust-colored edge which was beginning to shrivel them, and then, as soon as she could no longer be seen, actually running, fleeing through the deafening racket of the spar¬ rows, not going toward anything since it wasn't time yet, but fleeing the sound, the death rattle, the Vulcan's bel¬ lows wheezing, the noise of the forge, her heart pounding wildly from running, the blood's pulsations suddenly accelerating beating violently, her breasts rising and fall¬ ing while she stood there, motionless now, free from the death rattle, struggling in anger and rebellion against the bitter taste of tears, repeating: “No no," repeating: “She's nothing to me she can't she hasn't any right,” face to face with the cat crouching, flattened on top of the crumbling wall, the breach easy to step through from which she could see the turn of the road, but empty still, the sharp, yellow, fixed stare seeming to clutch at her, thrust into her like claws, the two of them like thieves caught red- handed, staring into each other's eyes, the pupils with the narrow, watchful slits in the briars' tangle, the thousands 105 of tiny leaves spreading, wavering ceaselessly, the branches weakly swaying, the clouds spreading, the con¬ tinuous hum of whirling insects spreading, the interlacing stems of the wild sunflowers, the wild grass, the tongues of the grass licking her bare legs, and finally the cat turn¬ ing away abruptly, turning away its head, no longer looking at her, denying her, effacing her, suppressing her not only from its consciousness but from the world, losing interest in her as if she had suddenly lost all existence, coming alive, stretching, beginning to walk, casual, its supple back undulating along the top of the wall, then jumping down on the other side, disappearing, and she (still able to see herself with that perspective which remoteness in time affords, free from the subjection of the present, watching herself act with that kind of half-scorn¬ ful, half-irritated, slightly envious condescension we feel toward ourselves when we see ourselves after the fact, as we would watch a child act, unaware of what we know, have learned in the light of what has happened since, as if knowing the future conferred a superiority upon us, whereas all we have gained is perhaps to have a few less illusions, a little less innocence, so that it has not been a gain at all, but a loss) standing there alone, the sun's rays increasingly horizontal, the darkness filling the valley, the fields, the road, the turn, rising slowly like a tide, the top of the tallest tree still in sunlight for a moment, golden, fiery, then fading too, and the car—the gray Simca— taking the turn, slowing down, disappearing again, but 106 she still not moving, listening to the racket of the spar¬ rows gradually die down, a dog barking somewhere near the river, one of those two-speed pumps gasping to raise the water in a garden, the water murmuring, fragments of sky running down the parallel ruts, the wet smell of the earth rising, the peace, the night rising, spreading, a faint bluish mist over the river blurring the fields, the western sky turning from rust to green, then slate, the leaves completely black now silhouetted against it while she could hear their two voices whispering, hasty and uneasy, she saying: “What?” and he: “Have you decided?” and she: “Decided?” and he: “About us I,” and she: “Decided I decided a long time ago and nothing will make me,” and he: “I,” and she: “Yes yes yes,” her voice harsh, violent, still full of that gasping rage, and just then the windows lighting up (now the house is simply a black mass over their heads, among the black shapes of the motionless trees, the black and motionless bushes, the clump of bamboos black and motionless too where the sparrows have finally stopped now, the house itself like a huge tousled bird, asleep in the middle of the lawn), the rectangles of orange light brutally silhouetted in the twi¬ light that is already almost night, and she: “I have to,” and he repeating: "Well?,” not releasing her from his em¬ brace and she twisting her shoulders to release herself: “Yes it's yes I told you yes well?” Pulling free, pushing him back, releasing herself . . . And she could see herself walking into the dining-room, 107 the scene, the tableau: Sabine and the fat man already sitting down (but the chair at the fourth place still empty) both looking up as she came in with, on their faces, the same questioning, vaguely frightened expression—or per¬ haps not: merely because she was coming out of the dark¬ ness, the shadows, blinking, discovering in the exact light the two faces turned toward her as though surprised by one of those brutal flash bulbs, the wrinkles like lines of demarcation drawn between the different parts of the faces, as if the latter were already no more than a mass of flesh ready to come apart (as on those diagrams where dotted lines on the bodies of cattle show the different cuts as they will be hanging later in the butcher's stall), the old couple (or rather the old man and the woman who refused to consider herself old, who continued or rather insisted on, struggled for, clung to that impossible preser¬ vation, with her gaudy dress, her blood-red nails, her painted face under the violent make-up like the faces of old whores: vaguely frightening, postulating not the idea of pleasure or sensuousness but of some primitive, barbar¬ ous cult: the ancestor, the venerable grandfather of the world, the ancient phallus decorated with garlands, rising monstrous, solitary, and enormous with its blind head, its blind eye, its stony rigidity (and, in the background, doves, offerings, animals sacrificed, crowned with flowers, slow processions); something to be written—-or described —in Latin, with the help of those Latin words which are not raw and improper but, apparently, specially conceived 108 and created for bronze, the cemented stones of triumphal arches, aqueducts, monuments, the rows of words them¬ selves cemented together, themselves like indestructible walls destined to outlast time itself, with the compact succession of their letters cut into coins, cubes, rafters, evenly spaced, arranged without punctuation, in capitals, without the slightest gap, like those walls constructed without mortar, the words controlling one another, ordered too by that imperious syntax probably invented in the expectation of future mutilations and with the sole purpose of being capable of being reconstituted a thousand or two thousand years later, after being scattered, forgotten, buried, overgrown, submerged and rediscovered, spelled out by the hands of shepherds whose fingers trace the inscriptions on the marble pediment in the weeds of green Arcady, recited, stumbled through by the future genera¬ tions of schoolboys with inky fingers and burning cheeks, looking up (in the ink-stained dictionaries with dog-eared pages, with crumbling, patched, disjointed bindings, with blue or tan wrapping-paper covers, where successive gen¬ erations of older brothers have already looked up before them—a kind of Bible of knowledge, transmitted from hand to hand, and on the flyleaf the successive names of the owners in a long column, clumsily written in yellowed inks), looking up the old, the indestructible Latin words (matrona, menstrues, merit ulus), lips purple with ink nib¬ bling the pen as if, with the ink that smeared them, they were unconsciously sucking the milk, the principle not 1.09 even of a civilization, of a dusty culture with its futile and dusty books, but of life itself), the old couple, then, brought together here by the mere existence, the virtue, the functioning, the obscure, blind, and fecund oscillation of that indefatigable shuttle foraging since the beginning of time in the shadowy, obscure and secret vestibule of that tabernacle which is the gentle womb of women, and not only because, forty years ago, a young professor with pince-nez and goatee had asked in marriage (or had been asked in marriage by, or rather had been induced by her to ask in marriage) one of his students with a fragile, Dresden china face under the heavy mass of hair, but also because two old maids (but at the time they were not old maids yet), and even before them an old illiterate peasant, had decided to make a professor of the last of the children born, issued, sprung from that phallus they them¬ selves had issued from and which he (Pierre) possessed too (or which, rather, possessed him, that is, lived, grew upon him, making use of him somehow like common loam, thrusting its roots into him, deriving there the strength to grow, to become erect and cast its seed outside itself, and, for this sole purpose, requiring not only that this body —this loam—be fed, sustained, cared for, but even that the brain commanding this body think (and not only for itself, but for its seed as well, its progeny, its descend¬ ants ) of the means of palliating hunger, cold, sleep (and to an illiterate peasant condemned by his ignorance to spend his life bent over the dark soil, learning to read 110 must have seemed like one of these means, if not the only one), preoccupations consequently excluding all others not helping to furnish this unique organ (so unique that it is called “the” member of a man’s body, as if no other existed, or as if it summed them all up, commanded them all: the arms to work and feed it, the legs to carry it from place to place), to furnish it, then, with what was necessary, if necessary by violence, war, rape and—in a general way, if not as a rule—ruse), the old man and the old woman, then, looking up, spoon stopped half way between plate and mouth, mouth already open (that is, the man’s mouth, for Sabine, having read twenty years ago in some beauty or health magazine that soup was fattening, had ever since gone without soup, not that she had ever discovered—for she had continued to grow fatter regularly—any truth in the assertion, but probably out of a superstitious respect for the printed page), and, in their eyes, that vaguely frightened, vaguely reproving expression, until she heard her own voice (only without remembering if she had heard the question, nor even seen Sabine’s lips saying: “Where have you been?”), her own voice saying: “I walked down to the river. I needed I *> • • • But obviously Sabine didn’t hear her or didn’t bother to listen, either because she wasn’t interested in the answer or perhaps even because she hadn’t asked the question, for while Louise was sitting down, unfolding her napkin, she heard (not as if resulting from what she had just said, 111 but as if it were the consequence of what had been said before her appearance, her entrance into the room having, then, merely opened a parenthesis now closed, Sabine continuing): “I was just saying: about that emerald. Be¬ cause after all how does it happen that they found every¬ thing, all except two or three worthless things and, it so happens, just that one emerald. Of course I suppose you'll say it could have rolled into a ditch or down a hole but couldn't one of those men just as well have put it in his pocket or even have swallowed it, the way I read in the newspaper the Negroes do, or at least try to do, when they're working in . . . Georges and Julien say they stayed behind the whole time and kept their eyes on the men, but you know they were looking themselves, and it's easy to make a gesture like that without being seen. Because it certainly has disappeared. Of course we can't prove someone found it, of course we can't formally accuse one of those men, but it seems to me it must have been awfully tempting for one of them to . . ."
